newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat says will take tough measures on Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says will take tough measures on Jerusalem.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Monday he would consider tougher measures against Israel unless the Jewish state ceased provocative actions in Jerusalem
"Until now we are patient, but patience has its limits," he told reporters in Cairo after meeting Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and leaving for a visit to Moscow.

"Palestine is thinking of taking tougher steps to counter Israeli acts in Jerusalem and has already begun the process of submitting a memorandum to the U.N. Security Council. We are also considering calling for a meeting of the Arab League or even an Islamic summit," he added.
Arafat, who arrived in Cairo earlier on Monday, regularly consults with Mubarak on his peace negotiations with Israel.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Monday to strengthen Israel's hold over all of Jerusalem, saying he would decide within days whether to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in the Arab east of the city.
The Palestinians say Arab East Jerusalem is the capital of their future state while Israel argues that the whole city is its undivided capital.
Israeli officials in Jerusalem had drafted plans to build apartment blocks in Har Homa but opposition members said building on the site would reignite Arab-Israeli violence.
Both Egypt and Arafat have slammed Netanyahu's settlement expansion policy, saying it is the biggest obstacle to peace.
"The settlement expansion policy and confiscating Arab lands (are a few) of the bothersome practices," Arafat said.
He added that Israel had confiscated the identification cards of Jeruslamite Palestinians and was barring Christian and Moslem Palestinians from praying in their mosques and churches.
"Work is also still continuing in the digging of the tunnel beneath the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem...this is not only a Palestinian city but an Arab and Islamic one as well," he said.

Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed in clashes last year sparked by the opening of the controversial tunnel near the mosque, which is Islam's third holiest shrine. The clashes threatened to derail the whole peace process.
Netayahu's policies, which included his refusal to trade occupied Arab lands for peace, prompted the last pan-Arab meeting in Cairo in May.
Arafat called for an Arab League meeting late last year shortly after Netanyahu announced he was scrapping a ban on the expansion of Jewish settlements.

Although Israel has handed to Palestinian self-rule some areas of the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip, the status of Jerusalem has yet to be decided in final status talks scheduled to take place in a few years.

Arafat said he would visit Russian President Boris Yeltsin during his trip to Moscow, which along with the United States is a sponsor of the 1991 Madrid peace conference. The Palestinian leader is also due in Turkey, which came under Arab criticism for signing a military training pact with Israel.
